title: The crowd in Jerusalem teaches us one of the most uncomfortable lessons about human nature.
paragraphs: The crowd in Jerusalem teaches us one of the most uncomfortable lessons about human nature.

A lesson about praise.
A lesson about expectations.
A lesson about how quickly admiration can turn into rejection.
On Sunday, they welcomed Jesus like a king.

Palm branches covered the road.
People shouted with joy.
The city erupted with celebration.

“Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”
(Matthew 21:9)

It looked like victory.
It sounded like loyalty.
It felt like acceptance.
But only a few days later, the atmosphere in that same city shifted.
The cheers were gone.
And another cry filled the air:

“Crucify Him.”
(Mark 15:13)

The same city.
The same streets.
The same voices.
And that moment reveals something deeply important for every believer, every leader, every person walking with purpose.

Crowds are emotional.
But they are not always faithful.
Many people in that crowd loved what they thought Jesus would do.

They believed He would overthrow Rome.
They expected political power.
They imagined immediate victory and national restoration.
They wanted a Messiah who would conquer their enemies.
But Jesus came to conquer something far deeper.

Sin.
Death.
The broken condition of the human heart.
Instead of taking a throne in Jerusalem, He walked toward a cross.
Instead of raising an army, He carried a sacrifice.
Instead of fulfilling their expectations, He fulfilled the will of the Father.
And when Jesus didn’t become the version of Messiah many people wanted…
The excitement began to fade.
This is a powerful warning for our generation.
Because people often celebrate what benefits them.

They applaud when your life matches their expectations.
They support you when your calling aligns with their preferences.
They praise you while your obedience makes them comfortable.
But when truth confronts them…
When obedience becomes inconvenient…
When your calling refuses to serve their expectations…
Some of those same voices grow quiet.
Or worse — they turn critical.
Here is the lesson:
Not everyone praising you is committed to truth.

Some people celebrate moments.
But they do not surrender to the mission.

Some people love inspiration.
But they resist transformation.
Some people welcome the King…
Until they see the cross.
This is why Jesus never built His identity on the crowd.
John 2:24 tells us something remarkable:
“But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew all people.”
He understood the nature of public opinion.
He understood that excitement is not the same as devotion.
He understood that popularity can change overnight.
And if we are honest, we see the same pattern today.
Culture can celebrate something today and cancel it tomorrow.
People can praise you in one season and criticize you in another.
A crowd can lift someone up quickly…
And tear them down just as fast.
That is why building your identity on public approval is so dangerous.
Because applause is unstable.
Validation from people is temporary.
And popularity is never a reliable compass.
But Jesus shows us a different foundation.
He was not guided by applause.
He was guided by obedience.
He did not adjust His mission to protect His popularity.
He stayed faithful to the Father’s purpose — even when it led to rejection.
Even when it led to suffering.
Even when it led to the cross.
And here is the beautiful truth.
The cross was not the end of the story.
Three days later, the stone rolled away.
The crowd’s rejection could not cancel God’s plan.
Their disappointment could not stop resurrection.
Their misunderstanding could not silence redemption.
What they thought was defeat became the greatest victory in history.
So here is the deeper lesson many of us need to remember:

Do not let applause crown you.
Do not let criticism crush you.
And do not let the crowd define your calling.
Because crowds change.
Opinions shift.
Trends move.
But the purpose God gives you remains steady.
Sometimes obedience will make you misunderstood.
Sometimes truth will make you unpopular.
Sometimes faithfulness will make you walk a road that others do not understand.
But remember this:
The same Jesus who walked through the cheers of Palm Sunday also walked through the silence of the cross.
And He did not stop.
Because His mission was never built on the crowd.
It was built on the will of God.
So if you ever feel discouraged when people change…
When support disappears…
When applause fades…
Remember Jerusalem.
Remember the branches.
Remember the cross.
And remember the empty tomb.
Because the crowd does not write the final chapter.
God does.

Scripture:
Matthew 21:8–11
Mark 15:12–14
Luke 19:37–40
John 12:12–19

Reflection Question:
Have you ever experienced a moment where people celebrated you in one season but criticized you in another? What did that teach you about where your identity should come from?
